questions.q: A reset token is built as `${userId}-${Date.now().toString(36)}`. Why is it unsafe?
questions.explain: Hashing a guessable value does not make it unguessable: the attacker hashes their guesses too. A token must come from a secure random generator, 32 bytes for anything that grants access.
options: It is too short to fit in a URL
Nothing in it is secret: an attacker who knows the user id and roughly when the reset was requested can try every millisecond of that window
It is safe if the token is also hashed before storage

questions.q: A download link carries base64url(JSON.stringify({ attachment: 7, user: "ada" })). What stops a user from changing it to attachment 8?
questions.explain: Anyone can decode, edit and re-encode base64. A signed value adds an HMAC over the data, which only the key holder can produce.
options: Base64 is encrypted, so they cannot read it
The link is too long to edit by hand
Nothing: base64 is an encoding. The value needs a signature (an HMAC with a server key) that the server checks

questions.q: How many bits of entropy does a 6-digit numeric code have, roughly?
questions.explain: Each digit adds log2(10) ≈ 3.3 bits, so six digits are about 19.9 bits: fine for a code that expires quickly and allows few attempts, hopeless as a long-lived secret.

questions.q: What does this entropy calculator print?
questions.explain: Bits = length × log2(alphabet size), rounded down: a 32-symbol alphabet gives exactly 5 bits per character, hex gives 4, digits about 3.32.
questions.code:
const bits = (length, alphabet) => Math.floor(length * Math.log2(alphabet));

console.log(bits(6, 10), bits(10, 32), bits(32, 16), bits(12, 31));

questions.q: Why give tasks and invoices a random public id (like inv_5f2c…) next to the serial primary key?
questions.explain: Public ids appear in URLs and logs, so they are not secrets, but they should not be enumerable. You still need an authorization check on every request.
options: Sequential ids reveal volumes and invite trying the neighbours; random 128-bit ids are unguessable, while the serial key stays for joins and indexes
So the id can be used as a password

questions.q: What is the prefix in tokens like reset_… or lat_… for?
questions.explain: A recognisable prefix lets tools such as GitHub secret scanning flag an API key pushed by mistake, and lets your code refuse the wrong kind of token early.
options: It is part of the secret and adds entropy
It says what a string is, so you, your logs and secret scanners can recognise a leaked token; it is not secret

questions.q: Which of these may be used to create a session token?
questions.explain: Only a cryptographically secure random source makes an unguessable token. Math.random is predictable, and hashing predictable inputs keeps them predictable.
options: An auto-increment counter in the database

questions.q: What does this print about tokens made by @zudojs/crypto?
questions.explain: 32 random bytes are 43 base64url characters, plus the prefix: 6 + 43 = 49 and 4 + 43 = 47. 16 bytes in hex are 32 characters, plus inv_: 36.

questions.q: Why is a fast SHA-256 hash good enough for storing reset tokens, when it is wrong for passwords?
questions.explain: Slow password hashes exist to make guessing expensive. A random 32-byte token cannot be guessed at any speed, so the only goal is that a leaked table contains nothing usable.
options: A token has 256 random bits, so there is nothing to guess however fast the hash; a password is chosen by a person and can be one of a few million common ones

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: hashToken is the SHA-256 of the token as 64 hex characters, the same value sha256 gives. verifyTokenHash hashes the candidate and compares in constant time.

questions.q: In redeem, why is the reset row deleted before checking whether it has expired?
questions.explain: Deleting first makes "at most once" true in every path, including the failing ones. In SQL this is one DELETE … WHERE token_hash = $1 RETURNING user_id, expires_at.
options: So every token works at most once: an expired token cannot be tried again, and a valid one cannot be replayed
Because expired rows cannot be read

questions.q: The reset form answers "If that address has an account, we sent a reset link" for every address. Why?
questions.explain: Registered e-mail addresses are valuable to attackers for phishing and password guessing. The response, and ideally its timing, must not depend on whether the account exists.
options: A different answer for unknown addresses would let anyone find out which e-mails have accounts (account enumeration)
Because the server cannot know whether an account exists
It is required by the e-mail provider

questions.q: This store keeps one reset token per user and deletes a token when it is redeemed. What is printed?
questions.explain: Issuing b cancelled a. b worked once. c was redeemed too late, and because the row is deleted even when expired, the second attempt finds nothing.

questions.q: What does an HMAC prove that a plain SHA-256 hash cannot?
questions.explain: Anyone can recompute a plain hash of changed data. Only key holders can compute a matching HMAC. Proof that anyone can verify, without being able to sign, needs a public-key signature instead.
options: That the data was produced by someone who has the secret key, and was not changed since
That the data came from a specific person, verifiable by anyone

questions.q: What happens here?
questions.explain: The package refuses HMAC keys under 16 bytes: a short, human-chosen "secret" can be guessed offline from one signed value. Use 32 random bytes from the environment.
options: RangeError - HMAC key must be at least 16 bytes.
TypeError - key must be a string

questions.q: What is a "test vector", and why test an HMAC wrapper against one?
questions.explain: You cannot tell by looking whether a digest is right. A known-answer test catches a wrong algorithm, a key passed as text instead of bytes, or a wrong encoding.
options: A random input that changes every run
An input with a published correct output (for example from RFC 4231); matching it proves the wrapper uses the algorithm, key and encoding correctly
A benchmark of how fast the hash runs

questions.q: What does this print? (It is the standard SHA-256 test vector.)
questions.explain: A SHA-256 digest is 32 bytes, which is 64 hex characters, and the published digest of "abc" starts with ba7816bf. (a9993e36 is the start of SHA-1 of "abc".)

questions.q: Why compare an incoming API key with timingSafeEqualString instead of ===?
questions.explain: Over many requests an attacker can average the tiny time differences and find a secret one character at a time. Constant-time comparison removes that signal.
options: === gives wrong answers for long strings
=== stops at the first different character, so its time leaks how much of a guess is right; the helper always takes the same time
It hashes the key before comparing

questions.q: What do the constant-time helpers return?
questions.explain: Different lengths and invalid input give false instead of throwing. timingSafeEqualEncoded compares the decoded bytes, so upper- and lower-case hex for the same bytes are equal.

questions.q: A reset token is looked up with WHERE token_hash = $1, a normal (not constant-time) index lookup. Is that a timing leak?
questions.explain: Timing attacks need the attacker to control the compared value byte by byte. Hashing first destroys that control. This is one more reason to store and look up token hashes.
options: Yes, always use a constant-time loop over all rows
No: the attacker cannot choose what the hash of their guess starts with, so timing that depends on the stored hash tells them nothing useful about any token
Yes, unless the table is small
No, because databases are always constant-time

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: hashPassword refuses a cost below 16384 but hashes a 3-character password without complaint. The minimum length is your policy: check it with isValidPassword or a schema at registration.

questions.q: A stored password hash looks like v1$scrypt$16384$8$5$…$…. Why store the algorithm and cost settings with it?
questions.explain: The verifier reads the parameters from the stored value itself. That makes upgrading possible without resetting everyone's password.
options: So the password can be decrypted later
So hashes made with older settings still verify after you raise the cost, and you can re-hash them at the next login
So attackers know which algorithm to use

questions.q: What does the authentication tag in AES-256-GCM do?
questions.explain: Encryption without authentication can be tampered with silently. GCM is authenticated encryption: decryption either returns exactly what was sealed or fails.
options: It lets decryption detect any change to the ciphertext, the IV or the AAD, and refuse instead of returning wrong data
It makes the ciphertext the same each time

questions.q: Bank details are sealed with aad: utf8Encode("freelancer:17"). What does that stop?
questions.explain: AAD is not encrypted, but it is covered by the tag. Binding each value to its owner turns "swap two encrypted fields" into a decryption failure.
options: Someone with database access copying freelancer 17's sealed value into another freelancer's row: it only decrypts with the same AAD
Nothing; AAD is only a comment

questions.q: How many dot-separated parts does an envelope have, and what are the first two?
questions.explain: The envelope is version.algorithm.iv.tag.ciphertext. Recording the version and algorithm is what lets you change either later without guessing how old values were made.

questions.q: What is printed when the AAD does not match?
questions.explain: GCM does not say why decryption failed, and neither does the package. For your own stored data a 500 is right; for values a client sent you, catch it and answer with a generic 400.
options: Error undefined undefined Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data

questions.q: encrypt(plaintext, key, { iv }) lets you pass your own IV. What is the rule?
questions.explain: The package does not stop you from reusing an IV, so the safe habit is never to supply one. encryptEnvelope and encryptString without iv always use a new random one.
options: Always pass a fixed IV so results are reproducible
Use the current timestamp as the IV
Don't pass one: a repeated IV with the same key breaks GCM's secrecy and lets tags be forged, and the package generates a fresh random IV when you leave it out
Use the user id as the IV

questions.q: A deploy sets PAYOUT_KEY to a 5-byte value by mistake. What happens at start-up?
questions.explain: Loading the key refuses the wrong size at once, so the mistake is found at start-up, not at the first payout. The message states sizes, never the key.
options: CryptoError - Algorithm "aes-256-gcm" requires a 32-byte key, received 5 bytes.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's vault prefix every sealed value with the key id, as in 2026-09:v1.aes-256-gcm.…?
questions.explain: Key rotation needs old and new keys side by side for a while. Without the id you would have to try every key on every value.
options: So after a new key is added, each value says which key opens it: old values keep working, and a job can find and re-seal the ones on the old key
Because the key id is the encryption key
So the database can index it

questions.q: Which of these is safe to write to your logs?
questions.explain: A fingerprint is a hash that identifies a key without revealing it, so you can tell which key a server loaded. Keys, tokens and decrypted data never belong in logs.
options: The reset token from the e-mail link
The decrypted bank account number, if the log level is debug

questions.q: What is the right order for rotating an encryption key?
questions.explain: Every step keeps every value readable. Removing or replacing the old key first would make existing values unreadable.
options: Remove the old key, then re-encrypt everything with the new one
Add the new key and make it current; keep the old key for reading; re-seal old values in the background; remove the old key when nothing uses it
Replace the key in the environment variable and restart
Decrypt everything, delete the key, then encrypt again with the same key

questions.q: A signed value is checked in this order: format, key id, signature, purpose, expiry. Why check the signature before parsing the payload?
questions.explain: Verify, then parse, then act: the same rule as for webhooks. It shrinks what an attacker can reach to one HMAC comparison.
options: Parsing is slower than an HMAC
Until the signature matches, the payload is attacker-controlled; checking first means your JSON parser and your logic only ever see data you signed
The purpose is inside the signature

questions.q: Download links and e-mail confirmation links are signed with the same key. What goes wrong without a purpose field?
questions.explain: A signature proves you produced the value, not for what. Binding the purpose into the signed data stops cross-feature replay.
options: Nothing, the key is the same
A value signed for one feature is accepted by another, for example a download link replayed as an e-mail confirmation

questions.q: A signed download link is a bearer token. What does that mean for its design?
questions.explain: The signature protects against changes, not against copying. Short lifetimes limit the damage of a forwarded or leaked link.
options: Whoever holds it can use it until it expires, so keep it short-lived, put the user id inside, and never put secrets in the payload (it is only signed)
It can only be used by the person who received the e-mail
It must be stored in the database

questions.q: A partner must verify receipts you send them, but must not be able to create receipts. What do you use?
questions.explain: With an HMAC, anyone who can verify can also sign. A signature separates the two: the private key signs, the public key only verifies.
options: HMAC with a key you share with the partner
A public-key signature (Ed25519): you sign with the private key, they verify with the public key

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The naira sign is one character but 3 bytes in UTF-8. Anything you hash, sign or encrypt is bytes, so size limits must count bytes.

questions.q: Write randomToken(bytes) with the Web Crypto API (crypto.getRandomValues): fill a Uint8Array of bytes random bytes and return it as lower-case hex. Print the length for 16 and 32 bytes, and whether two tokens differ.
questions.explain: crypto.getRandomValues is the secure generator in both browsers and Node.js. Each byte becomes two hex characters, and padStart keeps bytes below 16 from losing their leading zero.

questions.q: Write inviteCode(): 12 characters chosen with crypto.getRandomValues from the 32-character alphabet ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789, grouped as XXXX-XXXX-XXXX. Because 256 is a multiple of 32, byte % 32 has no bias here.
questions.explain: With an alphabet of 32, every byte value maps to exactly 8 characters, so each is equally likely. With an alphabet of 31 or 36, % would favour some characters; randomFromAlphabet in @zudojs/crypto handles any size without that bias.

questions.q: Write hmacHex(keyBytes, message) with Web Crypto: import the key with crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", keyBytes, { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" }, false, ["sign"]), sign the UTF-8 bytes of the message, and return hex. Check it against RFC 4231 test case 1.
questions.explain: Matching the published vector proves the key, algorithm and encoding are right. hmacSha256 from @zudojs/crypto gives the same result with one call on the server.

questions.q: Write safeEqual(a, b) for two strings that does not stop early: if the lengths differ, return false; otherwise combine a.charCodeAt(i) ^ b.charCodeAt(i) for every position with |= and return whether the result is 0.
questions.explain: XOR is 0 only for equal characters, and |= remembers any difference without branching, so every comparison of equal-length strings does the same work. The length of a signature is not secret, so returning early on a length mismatch is fine.

questions.q: Finish verify(value, now) for values made by sign. Return "bad signature" when the HMAC does not match, "expired" when exp <= now, and otherwise the data object. Check the signature before parsing.
questions.explain: The edited payload keeps the old signature, which no longer matches. In production compare the two MACs in constant time (timingSafeEqualEncoded), and add a key id and a purpose, as the lesson's signValue does.

questions.q: Write loadKey(base64): decode the base64 text with atob into a Uint8Array; throw Error("encryption key is not set") for a missing or empty value, and Error("encryption key must be 32 bytes, got N") for any other length. Return the bytes.
questions.explain: Check keys once, at start-up, and fail loudly. The messages name the problem and the sizes, never the key. createCryptoKey does the size check for you in the real code.
questions.expected:
loaded 32 bytes
encryption key must be 32 bytes, got 5
encryption key is not set

questions.q: Write hashToken(token) with crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", …) over the UTF-8 bytes of the token, returning lower-case hex. Show that the hash is 64 characters and does not contain the token.
questions.explain: The same token always gives the same hash, which is what makes the database lookup work, and the hash reveals nothing about the token. hashToken from @zudojs/crypto returns exactly this.
